# Summarization {#sec-summarization}

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" icon="false"}
**Chapter status: drafted.** Every number on this page was measured on XL-Sum
Turkish [@hasan2021xlsum] — 27,176 training and 3,397 test BBC Türkçe
articles with journalist-written one-sentence summaries. The extractive
systems are scored on all 3,397; the LLM on a 500-article sample, stated
where it appears. @sec-summarization-rouge reports a tokenizer defect that
changes every ROUGE number ever published on Turkish, so the ROUGE used here
is written out rather than imported and validated against `rouge-score` to
ten decimal places on text that tool can tokenize. Software: `rouge-score`
0.1.2, `snowballstemmer` 3.1.1, NumPy 2.5.2 on Python 3.14.5; the local LLM
through `ollama` 0.24.0.
:::

**Learning objectives.** After this chapter you can:

- say which of several incompatible tasks the word "summary" is naming, and
  refuse to build one until somebody has chosen;
- characterise a summarization corpus before modelling it, and predict from
  that characterisation whether extractive methods can work at all;
- build the extractive baselines, including the oracle that tells you their
  ceiling;
- explain what ROUGE measures, what it cannot see, and why its standard
  implementation is broken for Turkish;
- distinguish intrinsic from extrinsic unfaithfulness and measure the rate of
  each;
- use an LLM as a judge while measuring the biases that come with it;
- summarize documents longer than the context window, and say what the
  pipeline loses.

## "Summarize this" is not one task {#sec-summarization-tasks}

Before any modelling, a specification problem that sinks more summarization
projects than any modelling choice. The word names at least four different
jobs, and the person asking usually has not decided which:

| axis | one end | the other end |
|:--|:--|:--|
| Audience intent | **indicative** — help me decide whether to read this | **informative** — replace reading it |
| Scope | **generic** — what is this about? | **query-focused** — what does this say about X? |
| Input | **single-document** | **multi-document**, where contradiction between sources becomes the hard part |
| Method | **extractive** — select source sentences | **abstractive** — generate new text |

: Four axes, sixteen tasks {tbl-colwidths="[20,40,40]"}

An indicative summary that is 80% accurate is fine; you were only deciding
whether to open the document. An informative summary that is 80% accurate is
a liability, because the reader is acting on it without checking. [Those are
different products with different acceptance criteria, and "summarize this"
distinguishes neither.]{.hl}

The first question on a summarization project is therefore not *which model*
but **who reads the output, and what happens if it is wrong**. Everything in
this chapter — including which metric to report — follows from that answer.

::: {.column-margin}
A useful forcing question when the requirement is vague: *"if the summary is
wrong, would the reader find out?"* If yes, you are building an indicative
summary and can tolerate error. If no, you are building an informative one
and @sec-summarization-faithfulness is the section that matters, not the
leaderboard.
:::

## Characterising the corpus before modelling it {#sec-summarization-corpus}

@sec-sequence-labeling made auditing the corpus a habit rather than an
accusation. Here the audit answers a question with immediate engineering
consequences: **can an extractive system work on this data at all?**

```python
# XL-Sum Turkish: BBC Türkçe articles, each with a one-sentence summary
# written by the journalist, not crowdsourced.
rows = [json.loads(l) for l in open("turkish_test.jsonl")]
```

```text
train  27,176 articles   median 303 words, 17 sentences   summary 22 words
val     3,397 articles   median 300 words, 17 sentences   summary 22 words
test    3,397 articles   median 296 words, 17 sentences   summary 21 words

compression 14x        83.4% of test summaries are exactly one sentence
```

The leakage check that dominated @sec-sequence-labeling comes back clean
here:

```text
train articles 27,176, distinct texts 27,173      3 internal duplicates
test article also in train                        0    0.00%
test url also in train                            0
test summary also in train                       24    0.71%
duplicate texts inside test                       0
```

[Zero article leakage.]{.hl} Worth saying plainly, because the habit is
easily misread as cynicism: you audit so that you can *trust* the numbers,
and sometimes the audit says you can. The 0.71% of repeated summaries are
BBC boilerplate attached to different articles, small enough to ignore and
large enough to mention.

### How much of the summary is in the article?

This is the measurement that decides the architecture. Following
@grusky2018newsroom, take each summary and greedily find the longest
fragments of it that appear verbatim in the source:

```text
coverage   0.527    share of summary words found anywhere in the article
density    1.05     mean squared length of the extractive fragments
novel     47.3%     summary words that never appear in the article
verbatim   0/500    summaries that are a copied article sentence
```

A density of 1.05 means the matching fragments are essentially **single
words**. There is almost no copied phrasing at all. For contrast, CNN /
DailyMail — the corpus most summarization intuitions were formed on — has
summaries built from bullet highlights that reuse the article's own clauses.
Running the identical measurement on 400 of its test articles makes the
contrast concrete:

| corpus | coverage | density | lead-3 R-1 | oracle R-1 |
|:--|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| CNN / DailyMail (English) | 0.845 | — | 29.44 | **40.58** |
| XL-Sum Turkish | 0.527 | 1.05 | 14.03 | **24.89** |

: The same code on two corpora, each with the tokenizer that is correct for
its language {tbl-colwidths="[34,16,16,16,18]"}

[XL-Sum Turkish is in the opposite regime, and the whole chapter follows from
that.]{.hl} These are *rewritten*, in the style @narayan2018xsum called
extreme summarization: one sentence, composed rather than selected.

::: {.column-margin}
The published lead-3 figure for CNN / DailyMail is 40.34 [@see2017get],
higher than the 29.44 measured here, because that number comes from the
original Perl ROUGE-1.5.5 with stemming and a truncated reference. The gap is
a preview of @sec-summarization-rouge's argument: ROUGE is not one number but
a family of them, and two papers reporting "ROUGE-1" are often not reporting
the same quantity.
:::

### Where the summary's content comes from

If the summary is not copied, is it at least drawn from the top of the
article? Matching each summary against every article sentence by unigram F1
and taking the best:

```text
best-matching article sentence, 500 test articles
  sentence  1:   79   15.8%  ###############################
  sentence  2:   54   10.8%  #####################
  sentence  3:   50   10.0%  ####################
  sentence  4:   38    7.6%  ###############
  sentence  5:   40    8.0%  ################
  sentence  6:   35    7.0%  ##############
  sentence  7:   30    6.0%  ############
  sentence  8:   30    6.0%  ############
  sentences 9+: 144   28.8%
```

Lead bias is real but weak: the first sentence wins only 15.8% of the time,
and **28.8% of summaries are best matched by something from sentence 9
onward**. A system that reads only the opening is throwing away most of the
evidence.

### A caution about that 47.3%

The novelty figure is inflated by Turkish, and by exactly how much is
measurable. Re-run it with the words normalized:

```text
summary words absent from the article
  exact surface form              47.3%
  after Snowball Turkish stemming 37.5%
  after 5-character prefix        32.8%
```

Between ten and fifteen of those points are **inflection, not new content**:

```text
summary 'bölgede'      <- article 'bölgedeki'
summary 'parlamento'   <- article 'parlamentonun'
summary 'uzmanlara'    <- article 'uzmanlar'
summary 'işgal'        <- article 'işgali'
```

Same word, different case, counted as different by anything that compares
surface strings. Hold on to that: it is a corpus statistic here, and in
@sec-summarization-rouge it becomes a defect in the field's standard metric.

## Extractive baselines, and their ceiling {#sec-summarization-extractive}

The extractive family selects sentences from the source. It cannot
hallucinate — every word was in the document — and it cannot compress below
a sentence. Full test set, 3,397 articles:

```text
system                    R-1     R-2     R-L    words   time
lead-1                  12.75    3.37   10.69     20.0
lead-2                  14.04    3.61   10.94     37.6    0.2s
lead-3                  14.03    3.74   10.44     54.9
random sentence          8.56    1.73    7.30     17.5
TextRank (1 sentence)   13.66    3.27   10.88     30.3   25.4s
oracle sentence         24.89    9.31   20.39     20.1    1.8s
```

Three things to read out of that table.

**Lead-3 is not strong here.** The received wisdom — "always report lead-3,
it beats trained models" — is a fact about CNN / DailyMail, where the same
code scores it at 29.44 R-1, and not a fact about summarization. On this
corpus lead-3 scores **14.03**, and lead-2 beats it. Adding a third sentence
adds 17 words and no information. [Report the lead baseline always; assume it
is strong never.]{.hl}

**TextRank does not earn its 25 seconds.** Building the sentence-similarity
graph and running centrality on it — @sec-clustering's machinery, no new
model — scores 13.66, between lead-1 and lead-2 [@mihalcea2004textrank]. It
is a real method and on this corpus it is a rounding error away from taking
the first sentence.

**The oracle is the number that decides the chapter.** The oracle picks, for
each article, the single sentence with the highest ROUGE-1 against the
reference — it reads the answer first, so it is not a system but a *ceiling*.
It scores **24.89**.

::: {.callout-warning appearance="simple"}
No single-sentence extractive system on this corpus can exceed 24.89 ROUGE-1,
because that is what perfect sentence selection achieves. The gap between
lead-2's 14.04 and that 24.89 is all the room there is for better selection;
everything above 24.89 requires *writing*, not selecting.

That is a corpus property, computed in 1.8 seconds, and it tells you whether
to reach for an abstractive model before you train anything.
:::

::: {.column-margin}
Run this oracle on any summarization corpus you are handed. If it is high —
CNN / DailyMail's is above 50 — extraction is viable and cheap, and you
should exhaust it before generating. If it is low, as here, the reference
summaries are compositions and extraction is structurally capped. Two lines
of code, and it decides the architecture.
:::

## What ROUGE measures, and what breaks it {#sec-summarization-rouge}

[ROUGE](#gloss-rouge){#term-rouge .term-ref} [@lin2004rouge] counts n-gram
overlap between a candidate summary and a reference. ROUGE-1 is unigram
overlap, ROUGE-2 bigram, ROUGE-L the longest common subsequence, each reported
as an F1. It has been the field's default metric for twenty years, and it
survives for the honest reason that it is cheap, deterministic and correlates
with quality well enough to rank obviously-bad systems below obviously-good
ones.

::: {#gloss-rouge .column-margin .term-gloss}
**ROUGE** — n-gram overlap against a reference summary, reported as an F1.
Cheap and reproducible; blind to whether the summary is true, and dependent
on a tokenizer nobody checks. [↩](#term-rouge){.term-back}
:::

This chapter has three complaints, in increasing order of how much they
should worry you.

### Complaint one: the standard implementation destroys Turkish

Google's `rouge-score` is the reference implementation. HuggingFace's
`evaluate` wraps it, and most papers reporting ROUGE since 2019 have used it.
Its tokenizer, reproducing the original Perl script's behaviour, is one line:

```python
# rouge_score/tokenize.py
text = text.lower()
text = re.sub(r"[^a-z0-9]+", " ", text)   # <- everything else is a separator
```

`[^a-z0-9]` does not include `ç`, `ğ`, `ı`, `ö`, `ş`, `ü` or `İ`. In Turkish
those are not punctuation; they are letters, and six of them are among the
language's most frequent. So:

```text
görüştü        -> ['g', 'r', 't']
çiğ            -> ['i']
köfte          -> ['k', 'fte']
değişiklik     -> ['de', 'i', 'iklik']
şehrinde       -> ['ehrinde']
Türkiye'nin    -> ['t', 'rkiye', 'nin']
```

::: {.anlp-widget}
```{=html}
<div class="widget-title">Run the tokenizer yourself — type Turkish, watch it disintegrate</div>
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof rougeTokInput = Inputs.textarea({
  label: "Turkish text",
  value: "Cumhurbaşkanı dün İstanbul'da iş insanlarıyla görüştü ve değişiklik sözü verdi.",
  width: 560, rows: 2,
  placeholder: "paste any Turkish sentence"})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
// the two lines from rouge_score/tokenize.py, transliterated
rougeTokenize = t => t.toLowerCase().replace(/[^a-z0-9]+/g, " ").trim().split(/\s+/).filter(x => x)
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
properTokenize = t => t.toLocaleLowerCase("tr").match(/[\p{L}\p{N}]+/gu) ?? []
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
rougeTokRows = properTokenize(rougeTokInput).map(w => {
  const pieces = rougeTokenize(w);
  return {word: w, pieces: pieces.join(" · ") || "(nothing left)",
          n: pieces.length, intact: pieces.length === 1 && pieces[0] === w};
})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
Inputs.table(rougeTokRows, {
  columns: ["word", "pieces", "n", "intact"],
  header: {word: "word", pieces: "what rouge-score sees", n: "pieces",
           intact: "survived?"},
  format: {intact: v => v ? "yes" : "NO"},
  width: {word: 180, pieces: 240, n: 70, intact: 90},
  rows: 14})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
md`**${rougeTokRows.filter(r => !r.intact).length} of ${rougeTokRows.length}**
words did not survive — ${(rougeTokRows.filter(r => !r.intact).length /
Math.max(rougeTokRows.length, 1) * 100).toFixed(1)}%, against the 44.4% measured
across 300 reference summaries below. Every fragment is still counted as a
token, and fragments match other fragments.`
```
:::

Measured over 300 reference summaries from this corpus:

```text
word tokens, correct Turkish tokenization    6,682
tokens after rouge-score                     9,660   1.45x as many
words left intact                            3,713    55.6%
words split or mutilated                     2,969    44.4%
average pieces per mutilated word             1.96
```

[Forty-four percent of Turkish words do not survive the tokenizer, and the
debris inflates every score.]{.hl} The single letters `g`, `r`, `t`, `i` match
each other across documents at random, so overlap goes up:

```text
system                  correct tokenizer    rouge-score default    inflation
lead-1                            12.75                  20.37        +59.8%
lead-2                            14.04                  22.51        +60.3%
lead-3                            14.03                  22.03        +57.0%
random sentence                    8.56                  15.44        +80.4%
TextRank                          13.66                  21.34        +56.2%
oracle sentence                   24.89                  30.28        +21.7%
```

: ROUGE-1 on the same 3,397 summaries, two tokenizers
{tbl-colwidths="[30,24,24,22]"}

Be precise about the damage, because overstating it would be its own error:
**the ranking is unchanged.** lead-2 > lead-3 > TextRank > lead-1 under both
tokenizers. What is destroyed is *comparability* — every published Turkish
ROUGE number is roughly 60% larger than the quantity its readers think it is,
by an amount that varies with how much a system copies. A random baseline
gains 80%; the oracle gains 22%. [The inflation is a function of the system,
so the gaps between systems are wrong even though the order survives.]{.hl}

::: {.column-margin}
Our own tokenizer needed a fix in the same family, and it is the bug
@sec-clustering found in the wild: `"İstanbul".lower()` gives `i` plus a
combining dot, which `\w+` then splits into `i` and `stanbul`; and
`"IŞIK".lower()` gives `işik` rather than `ışık`. Turkish lowercasing is not
`str.lower()`. Both directions have to be special-cased, and the bug is
invisible unless you print the tokens.
:::

To be sure the argument is about the tokenizer and not about our arithmetic,
the ROUGE used in this chapter was validated against `rouge-score` on 300
random ASCII-only pairs, where both tokenizers agree:

```text
max absolute difference vs rouge-score, 900 comparisons:  0.0000000000
```

The implementations are identical. The entire Turkish gap is tokenization.

### Complaint two: it depends on a normalizer nobody reports

Turkish inflects. `bölgede` and `bölgedeki` are the same word doing the same
job; ROUGE sees two unrelated tokens. Applying a stemmer before counting
moves every number:

```text
system                  surface   5-char prefix   Snowball tr
lead-1                    12.75           17.85         16.13
lead-2                    14.04           19.46         17.67
lead-3                    14.03           19.13         17.48
TextRank                  13.66           18.24         17.11
oracle sentence           24.89           29.30         27.77
```

: ROUGE-1 under three normalizers {tbl-colwidths="[28,18,18,18]"}

Five points of ROUGE-1 sit between "surface form" and "5-character prefix",
which is a larger difference than most papers' claimed improvements over
their baselines. **A ROUGE number is not interpretable without the tokenizer
and the normalizer that produced it**, and those are almost never stated.
This is not a Turkish problem; it is worse in Turkish.

### Complaint three: the one that actually matters

The first two complaints are about reproducibility, and could be fixed by a
convention. The third cannot be fixed.

[ROUGE cannot see whether the summary is true.]{.hl} It counts word overlap
with a reference, so a summary that copies the right words in a
truth-reversing order scores well, and a correct paraphrase using different
words scores badly. Consider a source sentence *"the minister denied that the
bank would be sold"*:

| candidate | truth | ROUGE-1 vs reference |
|:--|:--|--:|
| the minister denied the bank would be sold | correct | high |
| the minister said the bank would be sold | **false** | high — one word differs |
| the sale was ruled out by the ministry | correct | low — almost no overlap |

: What overlap cannot distinguish {tbl-colwidths="[46,18,36]"}

The false summary and the true one differ by a single token, and that token
carries the entire meaning. @kryscinski2019neural made this case at length;
@fabbri2021summeval then measured it, finding ROUGE's correlation with human
judgements of *consistency* to be weak enough that it cannot be used to rank
systems on faithfulness. @goyal2022news found human annotators preferring
GPT-3 summaries that ROUGE ranked *below* fine-tuned models.

So: report ROUGE, because it is the common currency and its absence looks
evasive. Never conclude from it alone. The next two sections are what to add.

## Abstractive summarization {#sec-summarization-abstractive}

Extraction is capped at 24.89 on this corpus, so the rest of the ground
belongs to models that *write*. Three framings have been used, and the
history is worth two paragraphs because it explains why the current answer
looks so anticlimactic.

**Encoder-decoder, trained on the task.** The encoder reads the article, the
decoder writes the summary, and the whole thing is trained on
(article, summary) pairs. BART, T5, mT5 and their descendants. This is what
"a summarization model" meant until about 2022, and it still wins on
throughput per unit of quality when you have a corpus and a fixed domain.

**Decoder-only, instructed.** @sec-pretraining's next-token objective already
teaches a model how text of every genre is shaped, including the shape of a
news lede. @sec-post-training is what makes the model *follow the
instruction* to produce one rather than continue the article. Summarization
turned out to be one of the tasks that needed no task-specific training at
all — the capability was latent in the pre-trained model, and instruction
tuning unlocked it.

That is why this chapter's abstractive system is a prompt rather than a
training run. It is also why @goyal2022news found human annotators preferring
zero-shot GPT-3 summaries over fine-tuned models that scored *higher* on
ROUGE — a result this chapter is about to reproduce in miniature.

```python
PROMPT = """Aşağıdaki haber metnini TEK BİR CÜMLEYLE özetle.

Kurallar:
- Yalnızca tek bir cümle yaz, en fazla 30 kelime.
- Sadece metinde geçen bilgileri kullan; metinde olmayan hiçbir şey ekleme.
- Haberin ana olayını ver, ayrıntıları değil.
- Başlık değil, tam bir cümle yaz.
- Sadece özeti yaz, başka hiçbir şey yazma.

Haber metni:
{text}"""
```

Two details in that prompt earn their place. The length cap exists because
ROUGE-1 F1 punishes long summaries through precision, so an uncapped model
writes three sentences and scores worse while being no less useful — a metric
artefact you have to defend against rather than discover. And the instruction
to use only what is in the text is the faithfulness constraint stated
explicitly; @sec-summarization-faithfulness measures whether it worked.

### What it scores

All six systems on the same 500 articles, ROUGE-1 with a tokenizer that
handles Turkish:

| system | R-1 | R-2 | R-L | words |
|:--|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| lead-1 | 13.24 | 3.36 | 10.85 | 20.1 |
| lead-2 | 14.69 | 3.79 | 11.16 | 38.0 |
| lead-3 | 14.52 | 3.95 | 10.74 | 55.4 |
| TextRank (1 sentence) | 13.92 | 3.29 | 10.93 | 29.8 |
| **LLM, zero-shot** | **19.29** | **6.00** | **16.08** | 23.7 |
| *oracle sentence* | *25.05* | *9.21* | *20.29* | *19.5* |

: Same 500 articles, surface-form normalizer {tbl-colwidths="[34,14,14,14,12]"}

The zero-shot LLM beats every real extractive system by about **4.6 ROUGE-1
points** and still sits **5.8 below the extractive oracle**. Both halves of
that matter: generation is clearly worth it here, and the ceiling on *perfect
sentence selection* is still above what a 9B model writing freely achieves
against these references.

Which should already make you suspicious of the metric, because a system that
picks the single best existing sentence is not obviously better than one that
writes a summary. @sec-summarization-faithfulness is where that suspicion is
confirmed with a measurement.

## Long documents {#sec-summarization-long}

The articles above are 300 words. Real summarization requests arrive as
80-page contracts, quarterly filings and year-long ticket histories, and at
that point the architecture stops being a model choice and becomes a pipeline
design.

Three patterns, in increasing order of what they cost and what they preserve:

**Truncate.** Feed the first *n* tokens and ignore the rest. Honest when lead
bias is strong; on this corpus, where 28.8% of summaries are best matched by
sentence 9 or later, it throws away most of the evidence. The cheapest option
and the one most often chosen by accident.

**Map-reduce.** Chunk, summarize each chunk, then summarize the summaries.
Cost is linear in document length, it parallelises perfectly, and it is the
default in every framework. What it loses is **anything that spans a chunk
boundary**: a contract clause qualified twelve pages later, a retraction, a
narrative arc. Each chunk summarizer sees a window with no idea what came
before, so it cannot know which of its details will matter globally, and the
reduce step can only work with what the map step happened to keep.

**Refine, or hierarchical rollup.** Carry a running summary forward, updating
it with each chunk. Preserves cross-chunk continuity, and is strictly
sequential — no parallelism — with the running summary drifting as it is
repeatedly rewritten. Late chunks get more influence than early ones, which
is the opposite failure to truncation.

::: {.column-margin}
The arithmetic that decides this is @sec-transformers'. Attention is
quadratic in sequence length, so one pass over 100k tokens is not ten times a
pass over 10k. Map-reduce trades that quadratic for a linear number of small
quadratic passes, which is why it wins on cost even where a long-context
model would fit the document — and why "the model has a million-token window"
does not settle the design.
:::

The rule that survives contact with production: [chunk on structure, never on
character count.]{.hl} Sections, clauses, chapters, speaker turns, dates.
A boundary drawn mid-argument produces two summaries that are each locally
plausible and jointly wrong, and that failure is invisible in every automatic
metric — it needs a reader who knows the document.

## Faithfulness {#sec-summarization-faithfulness}

A summary can be fluent, on topic, well-sized, high-ROUGE, and assert
something the source never said.
[Faithfulness](#gloss-faithfulness){#term-faithfulness .term-ref} is whether
every claim in the summary is supported by the source, and it is a different
question from whether the summary reads well or matches a reference.

::: {#gloss-faithfulness .column-margin .term-gloss}
**faithfulness** — whether a summary asserts only what its source supports.
Independent of fluency, independent of reference overlap, and the property
that decides whether anyone can act on the output.
[↩](#term-faithfulness){.term-back}
:::

@maynez2020faithfulness split the failure in two, and the distinction is
operationally useful because the fixes differ:

- **Intrinsic** — the summary misstates something that *is* in the source.
  Swapped subject and object, a negation dropped, two entities conflated,
  a number attached to the wrong thing. Detectable by comparing against the
  source, and usually a model error.
- **Extrinsic** — the summary adds something not in the source at all.
  Sometimes true (the model knows who the finance minister was) and sometimes
  invented. Detectable as *unsupported*; deciding whether it is also *false*
  needs the world, not the document.

An extrinsic addition that happens to be true is still a defect in an
informative summary, because the reader cannot tell which sentences were
grounded and which were supplied by the model.

### Counting it without a human

A crude proxy gets you a long way: **a number or a proper noun in the summary
that appears nowhere in the source is an unsupported claim.** It misses
intrinsic errors entirely — a swapped subject uses only source words — but it
catches extrinsic ones, and it costs nothing to run on every summary you
generate.

Crude proxies need a control, or you will believe whatever they say. The
control here is free: [lead-2 is copied verbatim from the article, so its
flag rate is the proxy's false-positive rate, and it must be zero.]{.hl}

```text
system                nums  unsupported   propers  unsupported   summaries flagged
lead-1  (control)      100            0       521            0       0    ( 0.0%)
lead-2  (control)      173            0       809            0       0    ( 0.0%)
```

Zero on both, which is what makes the next table worth reading. Getting there
took three attempts; the two failures are in @sec-summarization-proxy-bugs
because they are more instructive than the fix.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## The two versions of this proxy that were wrong {#sec-summarization-proxy-bugs}

**Attempt one** compared the summary's capitalised words against the
*capitalised* words of the source — and skipped sentence-initial ones in both,
to avoid counting "The" as a proper noun. So a name that appears in the
article only at the start of a sentence was recorded as absent. It reported
that **56% of BBC journalists' own summaries were unfaithful**, which is the
kind of number that should stop you rather than excite you.

**Attempt two** fixed that by checking the whole source, but built the
summary's token set with `str.split()` while building the source's with
`\w+`. So `İtalya'ya` in the summary never matched `italya` in the source,
`neo-İslamcı` never matched `islamcı`, and a source typo like
`Komisyonu,hemşirenin` matched nothing at all. Copied text — which cannot be
unfaithful — came back 8% unfaithful.

Both bugs share a shape: **the two sides of a comparison were tokenised
differently.** That is the same defect @sec-summarization-rouge finds in
`rouge-score` and the same one @sec-sequence-labeling found in an LLM
extraction pipeline. When a metric compares text against text, the first
thing to check is that both sides went through the same tokenizer, and the
cheapest way to check is a control whose answer you already know.
:::

### What the proxy found

::: {.callout-warning appearance="simple"}
The most surprising number in this chapter is not about a model.

```text
system                nums  unsupported   propers  unsupported   summaries flagged
lead-1  (control)      100            0       521            0       0    ( 0.0%)
lead-2  (control)      173            0       809            0       0    ( 0.0%)
LLM (qwen3.5:9b)        61            0       494            3       3    ( 2.0%)
reference (human)       74           33       644          173      86    (57.3%)
```
:::

[The reference summaries assert unsupported content at nearly thirty times the
rate the model does.]{.hl}

This is not a measurement error — the controls are clean — and it is not BBC
journalists inventing news. It is how the corpus was built. XL-Sum's
"summary" is the bolded intro line that accompanies the article, written to
orient a reader arriving cold, so it supplies background the body then takes
for granted: the minister's first name, the date of the referendum, the
figure from a report the article only alludes to.
@maynez2020faithfulness documented exactly this for XSum, which is built the
same way; here it is again in Turkish.

Some of the 57.3% is my proxy counting an abbreviation mismatch — the
reference writes *Avrupa Birliği* where the article writes *AB* — so treat it
as an upper bound. The direction is not in doubt.

Three consequences follow, and they are the reason this section is not a
footnote.

1. **ROUGE against these references rewards unfaithfulness.** A model that
   reproduces the reference's unsupported background scores higher. A model
   that refuses scores lower.
2. **Our prompt told the model to use only what is in the text, and it
   complied** — 2.0% against the reference's 57.3%. It is being penalised by
   the metric for doing the thing we asked.
3. **Fine-tuning on this corpus would teach a model to hallucinate**, because
   the training signal contains 57.3% unsupported assertions. This is the
   single strongest argument in this chapter against training on a
   scraped summarization corpus without auditing it first.

::: {.column-margin}
Which is also the answer to "why not just fine-tune mT5 on the 27,176
training pairs?" You can, and it will score better on ROUGE, and part of what
it will have learned is to assert things its input does not contain. The
metric will not tell you. @sec-data-annotation is the chapter on noticing
this class of problem before it reaches a model.
:::

## LLM-as-judge, and what it costs you {#sec-summarization-judge}

ROUGE cannot see faithfulness; a hand audit sees everything and does not
scale. The middle option is to ask a model, which is now the default in
practice [@liu2023geval] and comes with biases that have to be measured
rather than assumed away.

The design used here follows three rules worth stating, because breaking any
of them quietly invalidates the result:

1. **A different model judges than generates.** `gemma3:27b` judges
   `qwen3.5:9b`. Models prefer their own output, and a self-judged score is
   not a measurement.
2. **The judge answers one narrow question, under a schema.** Not "rate this
   summary 1-5" — *is every claim in this summary supported by the source?*
   with a two-value enum. A rubric with one axis is reproducible; a
   five-point overall quality score is a mood.
3. **The human reference is judged too, under identical conditions.** It is
   the only way to know what the judge's scores mean, and — as
   @sec-summarization-faithfulness showed — the reference is not
   automatically the ceiling.

### What the judge said

150 articles, both the model's summary and the human reference judged under
identical conditions:

| judged by | LLM (qwen3.5:9b) | reference (human) |
|:--|--:|--:|
| automatic proxy | 3.3% | 57.3% |
| `gemma3:27b` judge | 7.3% | 33.3% |

: Share of summaries with at least one unsupported claim, same 150 articles
{tbl-colwidths="[34,33,33]"}

The judge confirms the direction: **the human references are judged
unsupported four to five times as often as the model's summaries**. Two
methods, one crude and one expensive, disagree about the level and agree
about the ordering.

### The part worth more than either number

Agreement between the two methods, item by item:

```text
                       proxy flags   judge flags   both   verdicts agreeing
LLM (qwen3.5:9b)                 5            11      1        90.7%
reference (human)               86            50     35        56.0%
```

[On the model's summaries the two methods flag 5 and 11 items and overlap on
exactly one.]{.hl} That 90.7% agreement figure is almost entirely agreement
about the *clean* summaries; where either method sees a problem, they are
nearly disjoint.

This is what the theory predicts and it is easy to forget:

- The proxy can only see **extrinsic** errors — a name or number that is not
  in the source. It is structurally blind to intrinsic ones, because a
  swapped subject or a dropped negation uses only source words.
- The judge sees both, and adds its own errors: it flags the model at 7.3%
  where the proxy sees 3.3%, and it *clears* references the proxy flags,
  because it correctly resolves *AB* to *Avrupa Birliği* and the proxy
  cannot.

So: **the ranking is the trustworthy part; the rate is not.** Report both
measurements, report the disagreement, and if you need an absolute number —
"what fraction of what we ship is wrong?" — neither of these gives it to you.
That number comes from reading a random sample, which is @sec-data-annotation's
discipline and @sec-summarization-lab's step 6.

### What the judge costs

```text
300 judgements with gemma3:27b     20,482s     68.3s each
```

Nearly six hours to judge 150 article-summary pairs twice, against 20 minutes
to *generate* 500 summaries with the 9B model. [Judging is more expensive than
generating]{.hl}, because the judge reads the whole article as well as the
summary and you run it once per system. Budget for it as an evaluation cost,
not an afterthought, and sample rather than judging everything.

### The biases, and which ones this chapter measured

The design rules above exist because LLM judges have known, replicable
failure modes. This chapter's setup avoids two of them by construction and
does not measure the third:

| bias | what it is | handled here |
|:--|:--|:--|
| Self-preference | a model scores its own output higher | avoided: `gemma3:27b` judges `qwen3.5:9b` |
| Position | in a pairwise comparison, the option presented first wins more often [@zheng2023judging] | not applicable: this judge scores one summary at a time, with no pairwise ordering |
| Length | longer, more fluent answers score higher regardless of content | **not measured here** — the length cap in the prompt holds the model's summaries near the reference length (23.7 words against 21), which reduces the exposure but does not test for it |

: Judge biases and what this setup does about them {tbl-colwidths="[18,48,34]"}

Stating the third one plainly rather than waving at it: if you move to a
pairwise or 1–5 rubric judge, position and length bias both become live, and
@zheng2023judging's swap test — present both orders, count how often the
verdict flips — is the measurement to run before believing any of it.

## Summarization in production {#sec-summarization-production}

The engineering questions are the same three every generative feature has,
and summarization has unusually clean answers to two of them.

**Caching is nearly free money.** A summary is a pure function of
(document, prompt, model, decoding parameters). Key a cache on the hash of
those four and the same document is never summarized twice. Documents are
re-read far more often than they are written, so hit rates are high, and
unlike most LLM features there is no personalisation to defeat the cache.
Version the prompt into the key, or a prompt change will silently serve stale
output forever.

**Cost is dominated by input, not output.** Measured over the 500 articles
summarized here: **890 prompt tokens per article against 53 generated**, a
ratio of nearly 17 to 1 — and these are 300-word articles, the short end of
anything you would want summarized. For long documents under map-reduce the
ratio gets worse, because the intermediate summaries are read again. The
arithmetic is @sec-serving's: what you pay for is *reading*, so the lever is
how much you send, not how much you ask for. Truncating boilerplate —
headers, navigation, disclaimers, signature blocks — is usually a larger
saving than any model change.

**The human in the loop is a design decision, not a fallback.** Return to the
question from @sec-summarization-tasks: what happens if the summary is wrong?
Three shapes, in order of how much they cost:

| pattern | when | what it costs |
|:--|:--|:--|
| Show source alongside | the reader can verify in one glance | UI work, no per-item cost |
| Link every claim to its sentence | claims are checkable individually | the extraction of @sec-sequence-labeling, plus alignment |
| Human review before delivery | acting on a wrong summary is expensive | a person, per item |

: Who checks, and what checking costs {tbl-colwidths="[32,34,34]"}

[Showing the source next to the summary is the highest-return feature in most
summarization products]{.hl} and it is not a model improvement at all. It
converts an informative summary — which must be right — into an indicative
one, which only has to be useful.

## Intuition checks {#sec-summarization-intuition}

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 1. A vendor reports ROUGE-1 of 41 on Turkish news. Are you impressed?

You cannot be, until you know three things they almost certainly did not
state: the tokenizer, the normalizer, and the reference set.

On this corpus the same predictions score **14.03** with a Turkish-correct
tokenizer and **22.03** with `rouge-score`'s default, which treats `ç`, `ğ`,
`ı`, `ö`, `ş` and `ü` as punctuation and mutilates 44.4% of Turkish words.
Stemming moves it another five points. So "41" could be a strong system, or a
weak system measured generously, and the number alone cannot tell you.

Ask what tokenizer produced it. If the answer is "the standard one", the
number is not comparable to anything computed correctly.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 2. Before training anything, how do you know whether extraction can work?

Compute the oracle. For each document, take the single sentence with the
highest ROUGE against the reference, and average. That is what *perfect*
sentence selection achieves, so no extractive system can beat it.

Here it is **24.89**, and lead-2 already reaches 14.69 — so all the remaining
room in extraction is ten points, and everything above 24.89 requires
writing. On CNN / DailyMail the same measurement gives 40.58, which is why
extractive systems were respectable there for a decade.

Two lines of code, and it decides your architecture before you spend a GPU
hour.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 3. Your faithfulness metric says human journalists hallucinate in 56% of summaries. What do you do?

Not publish it. A number that surprising is far more likely to be a bug in
your measurement than a discovery, and the way to find out is a **control
whose answer you already know**.

Here the control is free: lead-2 is copied verbatim from the article, so it
*cannot* be unfaithful, and any flag on it is a false positive. Running it
exposed two bugs in two successive versions of the proxy — both the same
mistake, tokenising the two sides of the comparison differently.

Only after the control returned exactly zero was the reference's rate worth
reporting. It was still high (57.3%), for a real reason: the corpus's
summaries are BBC intro lines that supply background the article body does
not contain.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 4. Your model scores below the fine-tuned baseline on ROUGE. Is it worse?

Maybe the opposite. On this corpus the reference summaries assert unsupported
content in 33–57% of cases depending on how you measure, so ROUGE against
them rewards a model for reproducing that. Our prompt told the model to use
only what is in the text; it complied, and the metric charged it for the
compliance.

@goyal2022news found exactly this at scale — humans preferring zero-shot
GPT-3 summaries that ROUGE ranked below fine-tuned models. When ROUGE and a
faithfulness measurement disagree, the reference is a hypothesis about
quality, not the definition of it.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 5. You need to summarize 80-page contracts. Where does map-reduce lose?

At the chunk boundaries, and invisibly. Each chunk summarizer sees its window
with no knowledge of the rest, so it cannot tell which of its details will
matter globally; the reduce step can only work with what survived. A clause
qualified twelve pages later produces two locally-correct summaries that are
jointly wrong.

No automatic metric catches this — both summaries are fluent, both are
grounded in their own chunk. The mitigations are to chunk on *structure*
rather than character count, and to carry a running summary forward (refine)
when continuity matters more than parallelism.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 6. When is extractive summarization the right answer in 2026?

When being wrong is expensive and being clumsy is not. An extractive summary
is quoted text: it cannot assert anything the document does not contain, which
in a regulated or legal setting is worth more than fluency.

Also when the oracle says the answer *is* in the document — a high oracle
score means selection is viable — and when you need determinism, auditability,
or a per-document cost of approximately zero. Lead-2 on this corpus takes
0.2 seconds for 3,397 articles against 20 minutes for the LLM.
:::

## Interview questions {#sec-summarization-interview}

::: {.callout-warning appearance="simple"}
**On sourcing — the same caveat as @sec-text-as-data.** The questions below
recur in the two credible open sources this book uses throughout, plus the
ones this chapter's own measurements make answerable.
:::

### Testing whether you understand the task

**Q: How would you evaluate a summarization system?**

The answer that ends the question: ROUGE for comparability, a faithfulness
measurement because ROUGE cannot see truth, and a hand-audited random sample
with an interval because neither automatic measure gives you an absolute
rate. Then say what you would check first — the tokenizer, the oracle
ceiling, and whether the references themselves are faithful. Candidates who
answer "ROUGE" and stop have not shipped one.

**Q: Why is ROUGE still used if it is this flawed?**

Because it is cheap, deterministic, reproducible and comparable across
papers, and because the alternatives are expensive, non-deterministic, or
model-dependent. It ranks obviously-bad systems below obviously-good ones,
which is most of what a leaderboard needs. The honest position is to report
it and never to conclude from it — and to be able to say precisely what it
cannot see: faithfulness, and any paraphrase that uses different words.

**Q: Extractive or abstractive?**

Ask what the oracle says, then ask what happens if the summary is wrong.
High oracle plus expensive errors is an extractive problem. Low oracle plus
tolerant readers is an abstractive one. A candidate who answers from
preference rather than from those two questions is guessing.

### Testing whether you have shipped one

**Q: Your summarizer works in the demo and users say it hallucinates. Debug it.**

Ordered by cost, and the first two are not the model. (1) Is it actually
hallucinating, or is it surfacing something true the user did not expect?
Have them point at a sentence. (2) Chunking — a map-reduce boundary produces
locally-correct, jointly-wrong output that reads exactly like hallucination.
(3) The prompt: is there an explicit grounding instruction? Adding one took
the measured rate here from a model that was never asked to a model at 2–7%.
(4) Only then, the model and its decoding parameters.

**Q: How would you catch it automatically?**

An entity-and-number proxy is an afternoon's work and catches extrinsic
errors; validate it on copied text, which must score zero. An entailment
model or an LLM judge catches intrinsic errors too, at roughly 68 seconds per
judgement in this chapter's setup. Say that the two disagree at the item level
even when they agree on the ranking — measured here, an overlap of one item
out of the five and eleven each flagged — so neither replaces a sampled human
read.

**Q: 10 million documents, a budget, and a deadline. What do you build?**

Costs first: 890 prompt tokens per 300-word article, and input dominates, so
the biggest lever is boilerplate removal, not model choice. Then caching — a
summary is a pure function of (document, prompt, model, parameters), so key
on all four and version the prompt into the key. Then ask whether the reader
needs an informative summary or an indicative one, because showing the source
next to the summary converts one into the other and is cheaper than any model
improvement.

| `snowballstemmer` | 3.1.1 | Turkish stemming, for the normalizer comparison in @sec-summarization-rouge |
| `numpy` | 2.5.2 | the graph arithmetic behind TextRank and every average in the chapter |
| `ollama` | 0.24.0 | serving `qwen3.5:9b` for generation and `gemma3:27b` for judging |

: The stack these numbers came from. Python 3.14.5, Apple Silicon
{tbl-colwidths="[26,16,58]"}

Worth knowing about, not used above:

| library | current version | when you would reach for it |
|:--|:--|:--|
| `bert-score` | 0.3.13 | embedding-based overlap [@zhang2020bertscore] — survives paraphrase where ROUGE does not, and is still blind to faithfulness |
| `summac` / `AlignScore` | 0.0.4 / GitHub only | entailment-based faithfulness scoring: does the source entail each summary sentence? The principled version of this chapter's crude proxy |
| `factscore` | 0.2.0 | decomposes a summary into atomic claims and checks each one, which is what you want when the summary is long |
| `evaluate` | 0.4.6 | HuggingFace's metric wrapper — note that its `rouge` metric wraps `rouge-score`, tokenizer and all |

## Lab: summarize a corpus and find out whether anyone can trust it {#sec-summarization-lab}

Pick a corpus from your own domain with 200+ documents. Reference summaries
are optional — the point of this lab is that you can evaluate without them.

### Step 1 — decide what kind of summary, in writing

One paragraph naming the four axes from @sec-summarization-tasks and who
reads the output. If you cannot write it, the rest of the lab is premature.

### Step 2 — characterise the corpus before modelling

Compute coverage, density, and the oracle-sentence ROUGE. If the oracle is
high, build the extractive system and stop. If it is low, you have just
justified a generative model — with a number, to somebody who asked why.

If you have no reference summaries, run the oracle against the document's own
title or first sentence. It is a weaker signal and it still tells you whether
the answer is *in* the document or has to be composed.

### Step 3 — build lead-k and TextRank

Always. They take an hour and they are the numbers every later claim is
measured against.

### Step 4 — generate, with the length cap and the grounding instruction

Both matter, and both are in @sec-summarization-abstractive's prompt for
reasons this chapter measured.

### Step 5 — build the faithfulness proxy, then break it on purpose

Numbers and proper nouns absent from the source. Then run it on **copied
text** — lead-2 — and confirm it returns zero. It will not, the first time.
Fix it until it does, and keep the broken version's output; the difference
between the two is what you would have published.

### Step 6 — audit a random sample by hand

Thirty documents, read properly, each summary marked supported or not. Report
the rate **with a Wilson interval**, not as a verdict: 3/30 is 10% with a
95% interval from 3.5% to 25.6%, and shipping decisions differ across that
range. @sec-data-annotation has the sampling discipline.

### Step 7 — compare your hand audit against the proxy and the judge

Three measurements of the same property. Where they disagree, read the
document. The disagreements are the useful part — they tell you which of your
cheap metrics you are allowed to trust unattended.

### What to hand in

One table of systems against ROUGE, the faithfulness proxy and your hand
audit; the corpus characterisation from step 2; and a paragraph saying which
system you would ship, to whom, and what happens when it is wrong.

## Exercises {#sec-summarization-exercises}

1. **The oracle first.** On any summarization corpus you can reach, compute
   the oracle-sentence ROUGE-1 before building anything. Say what it implies
   about extraction, then build lead-3 and see whether the implication held.

2. **Break ROUGE deliberately.** Write two summaries of the same article: one
   true and clumsy, one false and fluent, where the false one differs from a
   correct summary by a single word (a negation, or a swapped subject).
   Compute ROUGE-1, -2 and -L for both. Report the ranking.

3. **The tokenizer, in your language.** Run `rouge_score.tokenize.tokenize`
   over 100 sentences in a language you know that is not English. Count how
   many words survive intact. If you work in Turkish, predict the answer from
   @sec-summarization-rouge before you run it.

4. **Normalizer sensitivity.** Take one system's output and score it under
   three normalizers — surface, stemmed, and lemmatized if you have a
   lemmatizer. Report the spread, and compare it to the improvement claimed
   by the most recent summarization paper you have read.

5. **Chunk-boundary loss.** Take a document long enough to need map-reduce.
   Summarize it whole, then under map-reduce with chunks that deliberately
   split a key argument in half. Find a fact present in the first summary and
   absent from the second, and explain the mechanism.

6. **Audit the references.** Run the faithfulness proxy of
   @sec-summarization-faithfulness against the *reference* summaries of any
   corpus you plan to fine-tune on. Validate it on copied text first. Then
   decide whether you still want to fine-tune on it.

7. **Cost, honestly.** For a corpus you actually have, compute the cost of
   summarizing all of it: prompt tokens, output tokens, wall clock, and the
   cache hit rate you would expect. Compare against the cost of the
   extractive baseline, which is approximately zero, and against what the
   summaries are worth.

## What to remember {#sec-summarization-summary}

- **Decide which summary before building one.** Indicative or informative,
  generic or query-focused, single or multi-document, extractive or
  abstractive. The forcing question is *who reads this, and what happens if
  it is wrong* — an 80%-accurate indicative summary is fine and an
  80%-accurate informative one is a liability.

- **Compute the oracle before choosing an architecture.** Perfect
  single-sentence selection scores **24.89** ROUGE-1 on this corpus and
  **40.58** on CNN / DailyMail. That one number, two lines of code, tells you
  whether the answer is *in* the document or has to be composed — and
  therefore whether extraction can work at all.

- **Do not inherit lead-3's reputation.** It scores 40.34 in the literature
  on CNN / DailyMail and **14.03** here, where lead-*2* beats it. Report the
  lead baseline always; assume it is strong never.

- **`rouge-score` mutilates 44.4% of Turkish words.** Its tokenizer treats
  `ç ğ ı ö ş ü İ` as punctuation, so `görüştü` becomes `['g','r','t']`. The
  debris matches at random and inflates ROUGE-1 by about 60% — unevenly, from
  +22% for the oracle to +80% for a random baseline. The rankings survive;
  comparability does not. Our own implementation needed a Turkish lowercaser
  for the same class of bug, and agrees with `rouge-score` to ten decimal
  places on text that tool can tokenize.

- **A ROUGE number without its tokenizer and normalizer is not a number.**
  Five points of ROUGE-1 separate "surface form" from "5-character prefix" on
  identical predictions — more than most papers claim over their baselines.

- **ROUGE cannot see whether the summary is true**, and on this corpus it
  actively rewards untruth: the human references assert unsupported content in
  **33–57%** of cases, against **2–7%** for a model told to stay in the text.
  Fine-tuning on such a corpus teaches a model to hallucinate, and the metric
  will report that as an improvement.

- **Validate a faithfulness metric on copied text.** Lead-2 is quoted
  verbatim, so it cannot be unfaithful and must score zero. That control
  caught two successive bugs here, both the same mistake: the two sides of the
  comparison went through different tokenizers. The first version reported
  BBC journalists as 56% unfaithful.

- **Two faithfulness measurements can agree on the ranking and on almost
  nothing else.** The proxy and the judge flagged 5 and 11 of the model's
  summaries and overlapped on **one**, because one sees only extrinsic errors
  and the other sees both. Trust the ordering, distrust the rate, and get
  absolute numbers from a sampled human read with an interval.

- **Judging costs more than generating.** 68.3 seconds per judgement against
  2.4 seconds per summary. Sample, do not judge everything, and never let a
  model judge its own output.

- **Input dominates cost.** 890 prompt tokens per article against 53
  generated. Stripping boilerplate beats every model change, and a cache keyed
  on (document, prompt, model, parameters) is close to free money because
  documents are read far more often than they are written.

- **Showing the source beside the summary is the highest-return feature in
  most summarization products**, and it is not a model improvement. It turns
  an informative summary, which has to be right, into an indicative one, which
  only has to be useful.
